topic.name: Calculating Areas Bounded by Parametric Functions

question.text: Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as \[ x = 2t^2, \qquad y = t + t^3 \] and the $x$-axis for $t \in [0,1].$
question.explanation:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve \[ x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2 \]

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

\[ \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we compute

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} & = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t} \left( 2t^2 \right) \\[5pt] & = 4t. \end{align*}

So, we obtain the integral expression \begin{align*} \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \,\textrm{d}t & = \int_{0}^{1} (t + t^3)(4t) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = 4\int_{0}^{1} (t^2 + t^4) \, \textrm{d}t. \end{align*}

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \geq 0$ for all $t \in [0,1].$

Therefore, the area is \begin{align*} A & = 4\int_{0}^{1} (t^2 + t^4) \,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = 4\int_{0}^{1} t^2 \,\textrm{d}t + 4\int_{0}^{1} t^4 \,\textrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = 4 \cdot \left.\dfrac{t^3}{3} \, \right|_{0}^{1} + 4 \cdot \left.\dfrac{t^5}{5} \, \right|_{0}^{1}\\[5pt] & = 4 \left(\dfrac{1}{3} - 0 \right) + 4\left(\dfrac{1}{5} - 0 \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{5}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{32}{15}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve

question.text: Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as \[ x = 2e^{-t}, \qquad y = 3\sin{t} \] and the $x$-axis for $t \in [0, \pi] ?$
question.explanation:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve \[ x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2 \]

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

\[ \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we compute

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} & = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t} \left( 2e^{-t} \right) \\[5pt] & = -2e^{-t}. \end{align*}

So, we obtain the integral expression \begin{align*} \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t & = \int_{0}^{\pi} 3\sin{t}(-2e^{-t}) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = -6\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin{t}e^{-t} \, \textrm{d}t. \end{align*}

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0$ for all $t \in [0,\pi].$

Therefore, the area is given by \[ A = -\left( -6\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin{t}e^{-t} \, \textrm{d}t \right) = 6\int_{0}^{\pi} e^{-t}\sin{t} \, \textrm{d}t. \]

example.title: Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve

question.text: Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as \[ x = (t^2 - 1)e^{t}, \qquad y = t^3+1 \] and the $x$-axis for $t \in [1,2] ?$
question.explanation:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve \[ x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2 \]

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

\[ \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we compute

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} &=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t} \left( (t^2 - 1)e^t \right) \\[5pt] &= 2te^{t} + (t^2 - 1)e^t\\[5pt] & = (t^2 + 2t - 1)e^{t}. \end{align*}

So, we obtain the integral expression \begin{align*} \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t & = \int_{1}^{2} (t^3 + 1)(t^2 + 2t - 1)e^t \, \textrm{d}t . \end{align*}

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \geq 0$ for all $t \in [1, 2].$

Therefore, the area is given by \[ A = \int_{1}^{2} (t^3 + 1)(t^2 + 2t - 1)e^t \, \textrm{d}t. \]

example.title: Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve

question.text: Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as \[ x = e^t - t, \qquad y = e^t + t \] and the $x$-axis for $t \in [0, e]?$
question.explanation:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve \[ x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2 \]

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

\[ \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we compute

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} &=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t} \left( e^t - t \right) \\[5pt] &= e^t - 1. \end{align*}

So, we obtain the integral expression \begin{align*} \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t & = \int_{0}^{e} (e^t + t)(e^t - 1) \, \textrm{d}t . \end{align*}

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \geq 0$ for all $t \in [0, e].$

Therefore, the area is given by \[ A = \int_{0}^{e} (e^t + t)(e^t - 1) \, \textrm{d}t. \]

example.title: Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve

question.text:
Find the area $ A$ bounded between the curve defined parametrically as
\[
x = t, \qquad y = t\sin(2t)
\]
and the $x$-axis for $t \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right].$ Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve \[ x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2 \] and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral \[ \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we compute \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} & = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t} \left( t \right) \\[5pt] & = 1. \end{align*}

So, we obtain the integral expression \begin{align*} \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \,\textrm{d}t & = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} t\sin(2t) \cdot 1 \, \textrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} t\sin(2t) \, \textrm{d}t. \end{align*}

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $\sin(2t) \ge 0$ for all $t \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and $t \ge 0.$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set \[ \begin{array}{ccl} u = t & \Rightarrow& u' = 1 \\[5pt] v' = \sin(2t) &\Rightarrow& v = -\dfrac{\cos(2t)}{2}. \end{array} \]

Therefore, we have \begin{align} \int_{0}^{\pi/2} t \sin(2t) \, \textrm{d}t &= -\dfrac{t\cos(2t)}{2} \, \Big|_{0}^{\pi/2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos(2t)\,\textrm{d}t. \end{align}

Finally, the area is \begin{align*} A &= \left|\int_{0}^{\pi/2} t\sin(2t) \, \textrm{d}t\right|\\[5pt] &= \left|\,-\dfrac{t\cos(2t)}{2} \, \Big|_{0}^{\pi/2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos(2t)\,\textrm{d}t\,\right|\\[5pt] &= \left|\,-\dfrac{t\cos(2t)}{2} \, \Big|_{0}^{\pi/2} + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(2t) \, \Big|_{0}^{\pi/2}\,\right|\\[5pt] &= \left|\,-\dfrac{\frac{\pi}{2}\cos\pi - 0\cdot\cos 0}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sin\pi-\sin 0\right)\,\right|\\[5pt] &= \left|\,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\,\right|\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}. \end{align*}
